what: The sections of this article, each with a line and a paragraph, for showing what the reader has already read. Built by admin/build/summaries.py from admin/content/articles/summaries/.

sections.label: The opening
sections.line: A follow-up to the maintenance deficit: who maintains the PHP you run, the services that should exist, and money that reaches maintainers.
sections.para: A follow-up to the maintenance deficit, with evidence. Every site switched off for php2shell either does not matter or someone must pay to maintain it. Buyers have no maintenance to buy; PHP's experts have no product to sell. Vendors resold the free fixes within a day. OpenJS shows a 15% revenue-share model. Seven services should exist now.

sections.label: In short
sections.line: Seven lines: two questions, both ways, the free fix resold, experts without a workflow, OpenJS, seven services, open source.
sections.para: Each switched-off site raises two questions: does it matter, and who pays to maintain it? Buyers cannot buy maintenance and maintainers cannot sell it. The fix was written free and resold by vendors within a day. The experts have no workflow to be hired. OpenJS has shared revenue since 2024. Seven services should exist, starting with bringing sites back.

sections.label: Two questions
sections.line: Either a switched-off site does not matter, or it matters and someone must pay to maintain it; measure the cost.
sections.para: Sites went offline because nobody could quickly say they were safe, since nobody was paid to know. No named source has estimated the php2shell shutdown costs; for Log4j, one US federal department reported 33,000 hours of response. Each organisation could count its own hours offline, affected users and staff time: the budget its maintenance should have had.

sections.label: A market failing both ways
sections.line: Buyers cannot buy maintenance of what they run; the PHP Foundation sells sponsorship logos; the packager works in their free time.
sections.para: Organisations running PHP budget for building, migrating and hosting, but cannot buy maintenance of their exact stack, so they switch sites off. The PHP Foundation sells sponsorship tiers from $12,000 a year with logos and an advisory seat, not support or maintained builds. The Debian and Ubuntu packager works mostly in their free time. Money stops with integrators.

sections.label: What happened to the old versions
sections.line: The security team published free source backports; Zend, Ubuntu, TuxCare, HeroDevs and Freexian sold builds; none states a share back.
sections.para: PHP 8.1 and older get no project releases, but the security team published free source backports for 7.4, 8.0 and 8.1. Vendors sold ready-made fixes almost at once. Only Zend appears among the Foundation's sponsors, at the Silver tier, and no vendor states a revenue share to PHP. The fixes were written by a donation-funded team and resold.

sections.label: It can work: the OpenJS model
sections.line: OpenJS's 2024 programme: project-endorsed partners sell end-of-life fixes and share 15% of revenue upstream.
sections.para: In May 2024 the OpenJS Foundation started an Ecosystem Sustainability Program: partners selling security fixes for end-of-life versions must be endorsed by the project's core team, and HeroDevs shares 15% of revenue with participating projects. Tidelift pays by usage, the Open Source Pledge asks $2,000 per developer, GitHub Sponsors passes on everything, but none is yet the default.

sections.label: Why the experts
sections.line: PHP's own developers are the best maintainers, but no workflow lets a buyer hire them for what it runs.
sections.para: Core developers and those around the Foundation know which fixes and back-ports are safe, yet a council or company cannot buy their maintenance of its PHP. From commercial experience, a maintainer tied to the source and serving many customers invests in scalable processes, tooling and tests that benefit everyone; a consultancy patching one site does not.

sections.label: The services that should exist now
sections.line: Seven services: bring sites back, maintained builds, patching on behalf, code removal, a dependency register, an incident desk, endorsed partners.
sections.para: Restore switched-off sites with reach mapping and patching, priced per site. Sell minimal, back-ported, signed PHP builds. Patch the CMS and plugins on each customer's copy. Remove unused code, easier in interpreted PHP. Keep a register of dependency, usage and maintainability that executives sign. Offer fast evidence-based assessment. Endorse partners with a revenue share.

sections.label: Towards regulation
sections.line: Make maintenance easy to buy first, then required through procurement line items and regulation.
sections.para: Foundations could publish how to become an endorsed maintenance partner and the share paid. Procurement could ask who maintains each open source dependency and how they are paid, with a maintainer line item. Regulation such as the Cyber Resilience Act, which holds manufacturers answerable for open source in products, could recognise endorsed maintenance as meeting that duty.

sections.label: Not only PHP
sections.line: The same holds for Node, Python and every runtime; this is about fixing open source's economics, not leaving it.
sections.para: PHP is this week's example, but every runtime and library faces the same questions: what we depend on, how much we use it, who maintains it, and how they are paid. JavaScript has a revenue-sharing model and Python a supported security role; most projects have neither. The aim is to pay the people who keep the code safe.

sections.label: What this does not claim
sections.line: The services are proposals; sponsor status is from one page; stated shares are not paid shares; some dates unconfirmed; no cost estimate.
sections.para: Pieces of the proposed services already exist, in vendor LTS builds and OpenJS's programme. Not shown as a sponsor refers to the Foundation's home page only. No stated revenue share is not proof none is paid. TuxCare's and Ubuntu's fix dates for some versions are unconfirmed. No shutdown cost estimate exists; Log4j is only a comparison.

sections.label: Where this comes from
sections.line: The memo, php.net, the PHP Foundation, vendor posts, Freexian, deb.sury.org, OpenJS, funding models and the CSRB report.
sections.para: Sources: Dinis Cruz's memo of 23 October 2026; php.net's advisory of 21 October; the PHP Foundation and its sponsorship tiers; Zend's post of 22 October; Ubuntu's, TuxCare's and HeroDevs' php2shell pages; Freexian's PHP LTS; deb.sury.org; the OpenJS programme announcement; Tidelift, the Open Source Pledge and GitHub Sponsors; and the Cyber Safety Review Board's Log4j report.
